topic: How many piano tuners are there in Chicago — and whose estimate is closest to the truth?
context:
The setting: a faculty lounge at the University of Chicago, 1953. Enrico Fermi
has just given a lecture on estimation under uncertainty. Five colleagues have
made a wager: $20 each into the pot, winner takes all. The winner is whoever
produces the estimate closest to the actual number, which will be verified
against the Yellow Pages by a neutral party.

The rules of the wager:
- No reference materials, no looking up statistics
- Every sub-estimate must be derived from quantities the estimator can
  intuitively verify from their own experience
- Each estimator must commit to a final number and defend it
- Disagreements about intermediate quantities are encouraged and will
  reveal whose intuitions are calibrated

What everyone agrees on:
- Chicago's population is roughly 3.5 million people
- The question is well-posed: we are counting people whose primary
  livelihood is tuning pianos in the Chicago metropolitan area

What nobody agrees on:
- How many households own a piano and how often they tune it
- Whether to count by piano count, tuner workload, or economic demand
- Whether the question is answerable at all without knowing the
  distribution of piano ownership across income brackets
expectations: Each agent must build their estimate from a completely different starting decomposition — no two approaches should share the same first step
The economist must model the supply side (tuner income, price per tuning, hours per week) AND the demand side and show they converge
The physicist must use order-of-magnitude reasoning and explicitly label which factors contribute most to the uncertainty
The biologist must find an analogy from biological systems (population ecology, resource carrying capacity) that yields a surprisingly useful estimate
The engineer must identify the single most common mistake people make when decomposing this problem and demonstrate why it introduces error
The philosopher must challenge whether "number of piano tuners" is a stable quantity at all — and must do so in a way that changes at least one other estimator's approach
The group must identify the single assumption that, if wrong by 2x, would change the final estimate by an order of magnitude
Every estimator must commit to a specific number with explicit uncertainty bounds before the conversation ends
The final comparison must reveal whose intuitions were most calibrated and explain why their domain gave them the advantage
deliverable: Chicago Piano-Tuner Estimation Worksheet: each participant’s distinct decomposition and assumptions, calculations, estimate and uncertainty bounds, the group’s final wager entry, and a post-comparison note on calibration and the most sensitive assumption.
